title: The Convention on Biological Diversity and Its Protocols

cards.b:
The CBD is the base of India's Biological Diversity Act 2002 and of global talks on nature. Prelims asks about its protocols (Cartagena, Nagoya), its targets (Aichi, Kunming-Montreal) and which body administers it.

Mains asks how India aligns national law with it.

Also remember that the treaty has no binding targets of its own; the targets come from decisions at each COP.

The Convention on Biological Diversity was opened for signature at the Rio Earth Summit (1992) and entered into force in 1993. India became a party in 1994. It has three objectives:

  • Conservation of biological diversity.
  • Sustainable use of its components.
  • Fair and equitable sharing of benefits from genetic resources.

The Secretariat is in Montreal. The COP is its decision body. The United States signed but did not ratify.

• Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (2000, in force 2003): governs safe handling and trade of living modified organisms (LMOs). Uses the advance informed agreement procedure.
  • Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit Sharing (2010, in force 2014): sets rules for access to genetic resources and traditional knowledge and sharing of benefits.
  • Nagoya-Kuala Lumpur Supplementary Protocol (2010): liability and redress for damage from LMOs.

India is a party to all three.

The Aichi Biodiversity Targets (20 targets for 2011 to 2020) were adopted at COP10 in Nagoya, Japan (2010). Most were missed. At COP15 (Montreal, December 2022) countries adopted the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework with 23 targets for 2030.

Key goals:

  • 30 by 30: protect 30 percent of land, inland water, coasts and oceans by 2030.
  • Restore 30 percent of degraded ecosystems.
  • Mobilise at least US$200 billion a year from all sources by 2030, and cut harmful subsidies by $500 billion a year.

• IPBES (2012) is the science panel, like the IPCC for nature.
  • GEF is the financial mechanism.
  • IUCN Red List tracks species status.
  • TEEB (2007-10) put values on ecosystem services.

COP16 was held in Cali, Colombia (2024). Check the latest COP for exams.

The Global Environment Facility channels funds, and a new Global Biodiversity Framework Fund was set up under it in 2023.

Genetic resources are material with real or potential value. ABS means a user, such as a company, must get prior informed consent and agree mutually-set terms with the provider country. Bioprospecting is searching nature for valuable products.

Biopiracy is use without consent or sharing. Famous cases: neem, turmeric and basmati patent disputes, where India challenged patents at the European and US offices. The turmeric patent was revoked in 1997 and the neem patent by the EPO (final decision 2005).

The CBD has no strong enforcement and the US is not a party. Rich countries want access to genes at low cost; poor countries want funds and technology. Digital sequence information (DSI) is a new fight: gene data online is used without sharing benefits. COP16 began a fund for DSI sharing.

Some say a legally binding target regime, like the Paris Agreement, is needed.

India implements the CBD through the Biological Diversity Act 2002, the National Biodiversity Authority in Chennai and state boards. India has a National Biodiversity Action Plan and a NBSAP update. The Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) blocks wrong patents on Ayurveda and Yoga. India hosted COP11 of the CBD at Hyderabad in 2012, where it launched the Hyderabad Pledge on funds.

• CBD: 1992 signed, 1993 in force.
  • Cartagena: 2000. Nagoya: 2010.
  • Aichi: 2010 for 2011-20.
  • Kunming-Montreal: 2022 with 23 targets and 30 by 30.
  • COP11: Hyderabad 2012.
  • Secretariat: Montreal.

India also announced a revised NBSAP aligned to the 2030 targets, and the Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act 2023 came after the Montreal deal.

Prelims-style: "Which protocol deals with LMOs?" (Cartagena). "Nagoya Protocol relates to access and benefit sharing."

Mains-style: "Discuss the importance of the Kunming-Montreal Framework for India." Structure: targets; 30 by 30; finance; India's laws and NBSAP; challenges (people, funds); way forward.

A sharp conclusion links the 30 by 30 target to India's existing protected area share of roughly five percent of land.

o: 30 percent of land and sea by 2030
